column2: Having finished the last chapter of Towers of Light, I truly feel as though a great weight has been lifted from me. Almost from the beginning of their serialization, Hu Xueyan and The Red-Topped Merchant received more generous praise from readers than they deserved. Once published in book form, they circulated among Chinese communities throughout the world. There were even many foreign readers who, unable to read Chinese, specially asked Chinese friends to explain the books to them. Yet something about this leaves me not knowing whether to laugh or cry: these readers hoped to learn Hu Xueyan's business techniques from my modest work. That was something I had never anticipated.

The writing of the Hu Xueyan trilogy has taken about as long as my daughter has been alive. Over these ten years and more, the course of Taiwan's economic development has continually prompted new reflections as I wrote. Of the reflections that have struck me most deeply, the first is this: the principal cause of Hu's failure was that, once Britain's Watt invented the steam engine and set the Industrial Revolution in motion, the decline of handicraft production became only a matter of time. Hu was not blind to this. But to preserve the livelihoods of the many silkworm-raising households in the Jiangnan countryside, he refused to change course. Nor was he willing to submit to the formidable economic power of the Western capitalist countries. His solitary struggle against their monopoly consequently led him into a crisis of cash flow. Hu was a national capitalist in the fullest sense. In modern times, he would certainly have received government support; the authorities of his own day had no such understanding. His failure may therefore be called a tragedy of his age.

Second, after his failure, Hu remained open and honourable, worthy of the name “Hangzhou Ironhead” from my native region. Looking at the economic crimes that have occurred so frequently in recent years, I wonder whether anyone might find in Hu Xueyan something to warn them and move them towards a better course.

My third deeply felt reflection is that Hu was a victim of the struggle between Li Hongzhang and Zuo Zongtang for political power and over the course of development. Anyone making an investment must consider the investment environment, and one of its most important factors is political stability. This may be another contribution of my work that I had not foreseen.
